$comment: The self-test corpus (HPS-46): deliberately broken index and case fixtures that every host's
corpus READER must reject. A fixture that passes is the failure. This proves the reader,
where the corpus proper proves the parser — the two are never mixed in one index.
Each case carries `selfTestFailure` naming the one way it is broken:
unknownExpectationKey  an expectations key NO host may ever consume. Keys prefixed
`selfTest` are a reserved namespace for exactly this purpose.
wrongTypeExpectation   a universally consumed key (`orderId`) declared with the wrong
JSON type — the accessor reads nothing, so an allow-list reader
stays green and an asserted-keys reader fails.
nestedUnreadExpectation  keys BELOW the top level of `expectations` that nothing reads.
The top-level key IS asserted, so a reader tracking only the top
level stays green; a reader honouring HPS-46b fails and names the
path. Both causes ride one fixture because the rule is that they
fail identically: a reserved `selfTest`-prefixed key no host may
consume, and a consumed key declared with the wrong JSON type.
missingFile            the index names a case file that does not exist.
malformedCase          the case file is not valid JSON and the case does NOT carry
`malformedJson` — undeclared rot, distinct from a deliberate
malformed fixture.
duplicateId            two cases share one id.
Top-level `orphanFiles` lists files present on disk but absent from `cases` — the reader's
directory sweep must flag them. The sibling directories `broken-index-json/` and
`broken-index-schema/` each hold an index broken at the index level (unparseable JSON;
parseable but no `cases` key) — a reader pointed at either must fail, not resolve to zero
cases.
check_manifest_conformance.py validates this set is well-formed-broken: each fixture broken
in exactly its declared way, before any host suite trusts it.
OWNERSHIP: maintainer-owned, same as the corpus proper.

cases.reason: An expectations key no host consumes must fail the suite, or a platform session's new assertion silently binds nobody (HPS-46).
orderId declared as a number. A typed accessor reads nothing from it; a reader that only allow-lists key NAMES counts it covered anyway. The exact asserted-keys bug.

HPS-46b. `items` IS asserted at the top level, so a reader tracking only the top level reports this case covered; the two keys inside the row are read by nothing. Deliberately the vault listing's shape rather than a manifest one — that is the blind spot the rule names, and the self-test corpus proves the READER, never the parser. `status` is the coercion half: a host reading it through an accessor that coerces across JSON types sees "404" and marks it read, which is the asserted-keys bug one level down.

items.selfTestNote: Prose at depth. Documentation keys are exempt at EVERY level, not just the top — a reader that only exempts them at the top reports this and is wrong.

cases.reason: A case whose file is gone must fail loudly, not be skipped as if it never existed.
Unparseable case bytes WITHOUT a malformedJson declaration are corpus rot the reader must surface, not data.
First half of the duplicate-id pair. Two cases with one id means one of them is invisible to id-dispatched suites.
Second half of the duplicate-id pair.
